title: It Came Upon the Midnight Clear
description: Edmund Hamilton Sears's Christmas carol in its UK version, to the traditional air "Noel" in the four parts printed in Church Hymns with Tunes (London, 1874), for 2 to 4 singers: verses 1 to 3 at a calm hymn pace. The tune turns to D minor at "Peace on the earth" and comes home quietly on "To hear the Angels sing."

credits.arrangement: The four parts in Church Hymns with Tunes (1874; music editor Arthur Sullivan), "Traditional Air rearranged", adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: Edmund Hamilton Sears died 14 January 1876 (Julian's Dictionary of Hymnology, as quoted at hymnary.org/person/Sears_EH); sung as Church Hymns with Tunes (1874) prints them, its verses 1 to 3 of four (the fourth, "O Prince of Peace, Thou knowest well", is not sung)
licence.tune: public domain: a traditional air, headed "NOEL. D.C.M. Traditional Air rearranged" in Church Hymns with Tunes (London: SPCK, 1874), its first known printing (Hymnary.org's tune page, hymnary.org/tune/noel_sullivan, says Sullivan "published it first in his Church Hymns with Tunes (1874)")
licence.arrangement: The four parts printed with the tune in Church Hymns with Tunes (1874), No. 82, signed on the page only "Traditional Air rearranged"; the book's music editor was Arthur Sullivan (died 1900), and Hymnary.org credits the adaptation to him (1874); public domain. The tune is the book's in its key and rhythm, apart from breaths, and the lower parts are the book's, with these changes for 2 to 4 beginners. One note a syllable in every lower part where the book moves within one: the tenor A3 on "It" (its A3, B-flat 3); on "the" in the first line the alto D4, tenor B-flat 3 and bass B-flat 3 (its quavers D4 F4, D4 C4 and B-flat 3 A3); the bass A2 on "their" (A2, B-flat 2), B-flat 2 on "in" (B-flat 2, C3), A2 on "ness" (A2, B-flat 2) and G2 on "the" in the last line (G2, F2); the alto E4 and tenor A3 on "emn" (E4 F-sharp 4, B-flat 3 A3), the alto G4 on "still-" (G4 E4) and F4 on "hear" (F4 G4); the tenor's dotted crotchet and quaver on C4 under "hear the" sung as two crotchets. So that 2 and 3 singers have each chord's third: on "That glo-" the alto sings G4, A4 (its E4, F4), the tenor E4 on "That" (C4) and the bass C3, F3 (B-flat 3, A3), so the duet has a third, not a bare fifth, on the downbeat; on "old" the alto A4 and tenor C4 (F4, A3); on "near" the alto D4 and tenor B-flat 3 (F4, D4); on "their" the alto A4 (C4, an octave under the tune); on "gold" the alto A3 (F4); on "men" the alto F4, a third above the tune's D4 (D4), and the tenor A3 (F3); on "cious King" the tenor G3, G3 (F3, E3), so the G chord loses the book's seventh, and the alto E4 on "King", a third above the tune's C4 (C4); on the pickup "The" the alto E4 and tenor C4 (C4, C3), so no part leaps more than a fifth into "world"; on "ness" the tenor C4 (C3), so it has no fifth down and octave up; on "on" in the first line (and its place in each verse) the alto D4 (F4), so the duet sings a third and the chord is D minor over F, not F alone; on "-ing" of "bending" (and its place in each verse) the alto D4 (F4), so the duet has no unison and the D minor chord is whole; and on the last "gels sing" the alto sings E4 and A4 (E4, F4), the tenor C4 and C4 (B-flat 3, A3), so the chord before the last has its third at every size (the book's seventh, B-flat, is left out) and the last chord has its root, third and fifth and its third at every size. Breaths written in for beginners: every part rests three quarters of a beat before each line; "clear" gives up a quarter beat before the book's quaver rest, the held "old", "gold", "King" and (in verses 1 and 2) "sing" give up three quarters, and "earth", "men" and "lay" are sung as quavers, the next line's first note coming a semiquaver late ("To" a semiquaver and quaver, "From" a dotted quaver). Not sung: the book's "A little slower" over the last two lines (the template has one tempo) and the Amen. Accepted exceptions, the book's notes kept: the alto doubles the tune's F4 on the pickups "It" and "To" (its only third, A3, would cost a leap of a fifth and back; the tenor has it at 4 singers); on "That" the alto's G4 leaves that chord without its third, E, at 2 and 3 singers, the price of a stepwise alto into "glo-"; on "emn" the one note a syllable leaves the D chord without its F-sharp; the tune's quavers on "the" (first line) and its B-flat on "song" (on the beat) over the alto's held D4 and F4 (an alto D4 under "song" would make octaves with the bass), and "the earth" in line 5 (a unison D4, then E4 over D4, the alto held under the tune's turn), give the duet a bare interval or a second, the trio having the third in the bass; the tenor's G3, F3 on "gels bend-" after its fourth down from C4 (every change made parallel fifths or octaves); the bass's octave G3 to G2 on "cious" going into the cadence; the E doubled on "on" in line 5 (A7 over E) and on "Heaven's" (C over E), where the music is in D minor and C major and E is not the leading tone; and the alto's crossings above the tune at "men", "King", "The" and the last "gels sing", reached by a third or a fourth, not a step.
licence.source: Church Hymns with Tunes, edited by Arthur Sullivan (London: Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, 1874), No. 82, "I heard the voice of many Angels", tune "NOEL. D.C.M. Traditional Air rearranged", pp. 62-63, in four parts in F major (one flat), common time, written here in F as printed, crotchet = 1; the music and words read from the University of Toronto (Robarts Library) copy at archive.org/details/churchhymnswitht00sulluoft/page/n83 and n84. The book gives no tempo; 88 crotchets is a calm hymn pace (the 1903 printing below marks minim = 108 in 4/2). The soprano's C4 on "King" and "The" is the tune's lowest note, two semitones under the beginner range: kept in the printed key, as G major would put the tenor's E4 and the bass's B-flat 3 over theirs. The words as printed there, with these differences from our US version's text (Hutchins, 1916): "Angels" capitalised; "Heaven's" (sung in one syllable, as the metre needs; US "heav'n's"); "unfurled" (US "unfurl'd"); "heavenly" in verse 2's third line and "heavenly wing" in its sixth (US "heav'nly" and "hov'ring wing"), each sung in two syllables as "heaven-ly"; "Babel-sounds" (US "Babel sounds"); "blessèd" (US "blessed"); verse 3 is Sears's "Yet with the woes of sin and strife" (the US version's verse 3 is "O ye, beneath life's crushing load"); and the 1874 punctuation, its dashes after "clear" and "bring:" left out. Compared with the later Church Hymns (London: SPCK, 1903; eds C. H. Lloyd and Basil Harwood), No. 90, "NOEL (First Tune). D.C.M. Traditional Air.", p. 144, in F, barred in 4/2, marked "By permission of Novello and Company, Limited" (archive.org/details/churchhht00soci/page/n183): its four parts are the same note for note where compared (the first line and "That", "near the earth, To", the fifth line and "still-ness lay", the tenor's C3 on "ness" included), and it holds "clear" through the 1874 quaver rest.
